questions.q: Why does computing historical average returns using only today's S&P 500 constituent list produce survivorship bias?
options: It includes too many companies, diluting the average
It only affects bond markets, not equities
It excludes companies that were removed from the index due to bankruptcy, delisting, or poor performance, overstating historical average returns
It uses adjusted close prices instead of raw prices
questions.explain: Companies that failed or were delisted drop out of today's constituent list entirely. Excluding them from a historical study removes the worst performers, inflating the apparent average historical return.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of look-ahead bias in a backtest?
options: Using log returns instead of simple returns
Using information in a simulated trading decision that would not actually have been known or available at that point in time
Using too few historical data points
Testing a strategy on multiple assets simultaneously
questions.explain: Look-ahead bias occurs when a backtest uses data that wasn't genuinely available at the simulated decision time — such as a restated financial statement, or ignoring realistic reporting lags.

questions.q: Why do hedge fund performance databases tend to suffer from backfill (instant history) bias?
options: Because funds often start reporting to a database only after establishing a good track record, then add their earlier history retroactively, while poorly-performing funds often never report at all
Because backfilling is a form of look-ahead bias applied to prices only
Because funds are legally required to report only good years
Because older funds use outdated accounting standards
questions.explain: Funds tend to begin voluntary database reporting once they have good results to show, then backfill history. Funds with poor early results are disproportionately likely to never start reporting, inflating the database's average performance.

A bias caused only by using too little historical data
A bias that only affects options pricing models
The tendency for some strategies, out of many tested against the same dataset, to appear profitable purely by chance
questions.explain: Testing enough parameter combinations or strategies against one dataset makes it statistically likely that some will appear 'significant' by pure chance, similar to p-hacking in other fields.

questions.q: Which practice most directly defends against both survivorship bias and look-ahead bias in a backtest?
options: Avoiding the use of adjusted close prices
Using point-in-time data that reflects exactly what existed and was knowable as of each historical date, including realistic reporting lags
Only testing strategies on the most recent year of data
Using the highest-frequency data available, regardless of its source
questions.explain: Point-in-time data reconstructs the actual historical universe (including later-delisted names) and respects realistic publication lags, directly addressing both survivorship and look-ahead bias.
